This is a RESEARCH AND PLANNING task only — no code changes, no implementation. Produce a thorough, concrete report/plan. Write your final, complete report to a file at /tmp/claude-0/-root/4f329df3-66ee-49c8-a6c5-615ecf189efc/scratchpad/discord-support-research.md (create the directory if needed) as well as returning it as your final answer — the file is so a human can read the full thing without truncation.

## The ask (verbatim from the owner of Nxeon, a VPS/hosting/game-server platform)

"Is it possible to create a discord server for nxeon with bots/mods that handles all the live chats, tickets, support messages, everything with customers. relays the info, and can also make replies which sends that info back through the nxeon system back to the customer. A fully automated contact support channel. I want you to do a deep dive on research on other features we should add and how exactly we can do this."

Unpack this into its real components: (1) is it technically possible to bridge Nxeon's existing customer-facing live-chat + ticket system into a Discord server, in both directions — customer message → appears in Discord for a mod/bot to see and reply to; mod/bot reply in Discord → delivered back to the customer through Nxeon's own UI/email, not just visible in Discord; (2) what a "fully automated" version of this could mean given Nxeon already has an AI live-chat agent; (3) what other features are worth adding once this bridge exists, informed by what other companies actually do.

## Part 1 — internal codebase audit (READ ONLY, do not modify anything)

Nxeon's existing customer support surfaces, as starting points (read these in full, follow their imports to build a real understanding — don't guess from names alone):

- `prisma/schema.prisma`: `Ticket` (line ~278) and `TicketMessage` (line ~290) models — read the full model definitions, every field, every relation.
- `lib/actions-support.ts` — the ticket system's server actions (creation, replying, status transitions). This session already established the exact DB-write sequence a ticket reply uses (ticketMessage.create + ticket.update status ANSWERED + notification.create + sendMail via emails.ticketReply) — confirm this by reading the actual code, don't just trust this description.
- `lib/actions-chat.ts`, `lib/chat-bot-step.ts`, `lib/chat-attachment.ts`, `lib/chat-typing.ts`, `lib/support-promise.ts` — the live-chat system. Find the actual Prisma model(s) backing live chat (search schema.prisma for whatever model these reference — likely something like ChatSession/ChatMessage, confirm the real name) and understand the current architecture: is it a widget on the customer portal, real-time (websocket/polling?), does it already have an AI-agent-first-response layer before/instead of a human?
- Search for any existing AI live-chat agent implementation (the codebase has one per this session's own memory — check `lib/kb-*.ts`, `lib/chat-*.ts` for an AI-driven auto-responder, tool-use loop, or similar) and understand exactly how it currently decides when to answer directly vs. hand off to a human, and what "handing off to a human" currently even means today (does a human have any interface for this right now? admin panel? nothing?).
- Check `app/admin/` for whatever admin-side UI currently exists for tickets/live-chat (e.g. `app/admin/tickets`, `app/admin/chat` or similar) — this is the thing a Discord bridge would either replace, supplement, or need to stay in sync with.
- Check whether any outbound-webhook or third-party-integration pattern already exists anywhere in this codebase (e.g. Slack, Discord, Zapier, generic webhooks) that a Discord integration could follow as a precedent for auth/security conventions.

## Part 2 — external research (use WebSearch/WebFetch; this space moves fast, verify against 2026 current docs, don't rely on stale training-data assumptions)

1. **Discord bot platform capabilities relevant to this use case**, verified against Discord's current developer documentation:
   - Bot permissions model, slash commands, buttons/select menus/modals (for a mod claiming a ticket, marking resolved, etc.)
   - Threads (Discord's "forum channel" type is specifically designed for ticket-like use cases — confirm current capabilities: per-thread membership, thread archiving, tags)
   - Webhooks (both incoming — Discord can accept an incoming webhook to post AS a message from an external system — and how a bot posts vs. a webhook posts, since they render differently and have different capability/permission models)
   - Rate limits realistic for a support-volume use case
   - Whether Discord requires special verification/approval for a bot serving external, non-Discord-native customers, or if there are ToS concerns with "using Discord as a headless support-ticket backend for a totally separate paying-customer product" — genuinely check Discord's Developer ToS/Bot policy for anything relevant here, don't assume it's fine.
2. **How comparable companies actually do this today** — search for how existing SaaS/hosting/gaming-adjacent companies bridge Discord with their own support/ticketing systems (many hosting/game-server companies specifically — this is a natural fit for Nxeon's own audience, who skew toward being Discord-native already per this session's own audience — Nxeon sells VPS/game-server hosting to a customer base that plausibly already lives in Discord). Look for concrete existing integrations/products: e.g. established helpdesk platforms with a "Discord channel" integration (Zendesk, Intercom, Freshdesk, Help Scout, Crisp, Tidio, Chatwoot — check which of these, if any, have a genuine bidirectional Discord bridge today, not just "post notifications to Discord"), and any open-source Discord-ticket-bot projects worth learning the architecture from (many exist for gaming communities specifically — e.g. "Discord ticket bot," "Discord modmail bot" patterns — these are a very close architectural cousin to what's being asked for, since a modmail bot already solves exactly "DM the bot → creates a private thread for mods → mod replies in thread → bot DMs the reply back to the user," which is structurally identical to "customer messages support → creates Discord thread → mod replies → customer gets it back through Nxeon").
3. **Whether "fully automated" is realistic** and what that actually looks like given Nxeon already has an AI support agent (per Part 1's findings) — research patterns for AI-agent-plus-human-escalation support flows generally (not Discord-specific), and specifically how an AI agent could operate INSIDE a Discord bridge (e.g., the bot auto-drafts a suggested reply for a human mod to approve/edit/send, vs. fully auto-sending AI replies with human-in-the-loop only on escalation, vs. AI handles everything and Discord is purely a monitoring/override surface for humans).

## Part 3 — synthesize into a concrete architecture proposal

Based on parts 1+2, propose (don't build) a concrete architecture:

- Data flow diagrams in words: customer opens live chat / submits ticket → [what happens] → appears in Discord as [what, exactly — a thread per ticket? a forum post? a message in a shared channel?] → mod/bot replies in Discord → [what happens] → customer sees it in Nxeon's portal / gets an email, exactly how.
- What needs to be built: a Discord bot application (new), a webhook receiver endpoint on Nxeon's side (new route, e.g. `/api/webhooks/discord`), whatever glue code maps a `Ticket`/chat-session id to a Discord thread id (a new join-table/field), signature verification for Discord's webhook payloads (Discord uses Ed25519 request signing for interactions — verify current requirements), and where the AI agent plugs in (before Discord sees it, or as a Discord bot itself responding in-thread).
- Security/privacy considerations specific to Nxeon: customer PII (email, order details, possibly payment-adjacent info) flowing into Discord messages visible to whoever has access to that server/channel — propose real mitigations (private threads scoped to a support-staff role only, redacting sensitive fields, an audit log, revoking a former mod's access model).
- A realistic phased rollout (e.g. Phase 1: read-only mirror of tickets into Discord for visibility; Phase 2: mod can reply from Discord and it round-trips to the customer; Phase 3: AI-drafted replies with mod approval; Phase 4: deeper automation) — with your own honest assessment of where the real engineering risk/effort is concentrated, and an estimate of what's a quick build vs. a substantial one.

## Part 4 — "other features we should add"

Beyond the Discord bridge itself, research and propose a concrete, prioritized list of other customer-support/community features worth adding, grounded in (a) what similar hosting/game-server companies actually offer today (research this, don't just brainstorm from priors) and (b) what would specifically complement Nxeon's existing real infrastructure (the live-chat AI agent, the ticket system, the customer base skewing toward Discord-native gamers/developers). Examples of the KIND of thing to research and evaluate (verify these are real, current practices before recommending them, and reject any that don't actually fit Nxeon's situation): status-page/incident-communication bots, a public Discord community server (separate concern from the support-bridge — a community hub with roles for customers, general chat, showcase channels) vs. a private support-only server, self-service Discord slash commands for common account actions (check server status, restart, etc. — but flag the real security risk of letting Discord identity map to account actions and how other companies handle that linking safely, e.g. OAuth account-linking flows), automated uptime/incident alerts to a Discord channel, referral/affiliate program integration, a public roadmap/changelog bot.

## Constraints on your report

- Every technical claim about Discord's current API/policies must be sourced (cite what you found and when) — do not state something as fact from training memory alone when it's the kind of thing that changes (rate limits, ToS terms, feature availability). If you can't verify something current, say so explicitly and mark it as "needs verification against current Discord docs before committing to this."
- Every claim about Nxeon's existing code must be grounded in an actual file:line reference from what you read, not assumed from the name of a file.
- Be honest about difficulty/effort — do not undersell what's a substantial integration project vs. what's a quick add. The owner explicitly wants to know "how exactly we can do this," which means real specificity (actual API names, actual Discord object types, actual file paths in this codebase), not generic consulting-speak.
- This is a genuinely open-ended research task — you have no time limit here beyond being thorough. Prioritize being right and specific over being fast.

168	  message: string;
169	  history: ClaudeMessage[];
170	  chunks: LlmChunk[];
171	  images?: LlmImage[];
172	  visitorName?: string | null;
173	  userId?: string | null;

178	}): Promise<LlmResult> {
179	  const key = await resolveBotKey();
180	  if (!key) return { ok: false, reason: "no_key" };
181	
182	  const accountAware = Boolean(args.userId);
183	  const uid = args.userId ?? null;
184	  const [model, coupon] = await Promise.all([
185	    getSetting("kb_bot_model", DEFAULT_BOT_MODEL),
186	    getSetting("kb_bot_coupon", ""),
187	  ]);
188	
189	  // A light pre-fetch of relevant help snippets seeds the first turn; the model
190	  // can also call search_help to dig deeper. Snippets are CONTEXT, never the
191	  // answer — the prompt forbids pasting them.
192	  const context = args.chunks.length
193	    ? "=== POSSIBLY-RELEVANT HELP SNIPPETS (context only — rewrite in your own words, never paste) ===\n" +
194	      args.chunks
195	        .map(
196	          (c) =>
197	            `• ${c.title}\n${c.snippet}${c.url ? `\n(link: ${c.url.startsWith("http") ? c.url : APP_URL + c.url})` : ""}`,
198	        )

200	    : "";

202	  const base = buildSystem(coupon, args.visitorName ?? null, accountAware);

206	  // needs a text block so the model knows what to do with the picture.
207	  const imgs = args.images ?? [];
208	  const currentContent: ClaudeContent = imgs.length
209	    ? [

211	          type: "image" as const,
212	          source: { type: "base64" as const, media_type: im.mediaType, data: im.dataB64 },
213	        })),

231	      messages,

242	    return { ok: true, text: trimmedText };

245	    // API outage) AND degrade gracefully — NEVER silently fall to blog snippets.
246	    return { ok: false, reason: "error", detail: e instanceof Error ? e.message : "chat model error" };

249	    // a stale "Checking your billing…" can never bleed into the next turn's
250	    // pre-tool-call gap or linger after the reply has already rendered.
251	    if (convoId) clearBotStep(convoId);

## Key Changes as of June 2026

As of June 10th, 2026, Discord made changes to the Privileged Intents review process. The threshold has shifted significantly:

**Old System (Pre-June 2026):**
Previously, apps in fewer than 100 servers could access Privileged Intents by toggling them on in the Developer Portal, and apps in 100+ servers needed to apply for access.

**New System (June 2026 onwards):**
The threshold is now based on the number of unique users who can see your app across all the servers it's in. If that number exceeds 10,000, your app needs to apply for Privileged Intent access. ## Security Headers

Every interaction request is sent with the X-Signature-Ed25519 header as a signature and X-Signature-Timestamp header as a timestamp.

## Validation Requirements

Your Interactions Endpoint URL must validate the security-related request headers (X-Signature-Ed25519 and X-Signature-Timestamp). If the signature fails validation, respond with a 401 error code.

## Verification Process

To validate headers, you concatenate the timestamp and raw request body, then use Ed25519 signature verification with your application's public key. The verification process involves:

1. Extracting the `X-Signature-Ed25519` and `X-Signature-Timestamp` headers from the request
2. Concatenating the timestamp with the raw request body
3. Verifying the signature using your application's public key

Example code shows extracting the signature and timestamp using `req.get('X-Signature-Ed25519')` and `req.get('X-Signature-Timestamp')`, then calling verifyKey with the raw body, signature, timestamp, and your client public key.

## Important Notes

If you are not properly validating this signature header, Discord will not allow you to save your interactions URL in the Developer Portal. Discord also does automated, routine security checks against your endpoint, including purposefully sending invalid signatures.

# Nxeon × Discord Support Bridge — Deep-Dive Research & Architecture Plan

## Executive summary

Yes, it's technically possible, but "fully automated Discord does everything" is the wrong framing — Nxeon already has a live-chat AI agent, a ticket system, and a full admin inbox UI (`/admin/chat`, `/admin/support`). Discord would become **a new front-end/relay surface for staff**, not a replacement backend. The real engineering questions are (1) how a `Ticket`/`ChatConversation` row gets mirrored into a Discord channel/thread, (2) how a reply typed in Discord gets back into the DB and out to the customer, and (3) where the AI agent sits in that loop. None of this requires abandoning the existing polling architecture — in fact the cleanest design leans on the exact same polling pattern already used everywhere else in this codebase, avoiding the need to stand up a new always-on Discord Gateway process.

Two structurally different asks got bundled together in the owner's message and need separating:
- **(A) Staff-side relay/bridge**: customers keep using the Nxeon widget/portal; Discord is where *staff* see and answer, and stays invisible to customers. No Discord account needed by any customer. This is the higher-value, lower-risk build.
- **(B) Discord as a customer-facing support entry point** (customer DMs a bot or opens a ticket inside a public/community Discord server) — the classic "modmail bot" pattern. This is a second, optional channel, not a requirement, and raises real identity-linking and PII questions Nxeon doesn't have today.

The report below covers the codebase audit, the sourced Discord platform research, a concrete phased architecture for (A) with (B) as an optional extension, and a prioritized "what else to build" list.

---

## Part 1 — Internal codebase audit (grounded in real files)

### 1.1 Ticket system — `prisma/schema.prisma`, `lib/actions-support.ts`

`Ticket` (`prisma/schema.prisma:278-288`) and `TicketMessage` (`prisma/schema.prisma:290-299`) are simple:

```
model Ticket {
  id, subject, status: TicketStatus (OPEN|ANSWERED|CUSTOMER_REPLY|CLOSED),
  priority: TicketPriority (LOW|NORMAL|HIGH|URGENT), userId, messages[], createdAt, updatedAt
}
model TicketMessage {
  id, body, isStaff: Boolean, ticketId, authorId, createdAt
}
```
No `assignedToId`, no external-reference field, no attachment relation on tickets today (chat has attachments; tickets don't) — any Discord bridge needs a new field to store the Discord channel/thread id per ticket (see §3).

`lib/actions-support.ts` confirmed exactly the write sequence described in the prompt, with one correction worth flagging: **`replyTicket` (lines 87-149)** does the following inside `db.$transaction`:
1. `db.ticketMessage.create({ ticketId, body, authorId, isStaff })`
2. `db.ticket.update({ status: isStaff ? "ANSWERED" : "CUSTOMER_REPLY" })`

Then, *outside* the transaction, if `isStaff`:
3. `db.notification.create(...)` to the ticket owner (in-app bell)
4. best-effort `sendMail({ ..., template: tpl.template, kind: "support_reply" })` using `emails.ticketReply()` from `lib/email-templates.ts:851-863` — **wrapped in try/catch so a mail failure never fails the reply** (line 133-135).

`emails.ticketReply` (`lib/email-templates.ts:851`) is a **notification-only** email: subject `[#<id>] New reply: <subject>`, a body preview, and a CTA link back to `/dashboard/support`. There is **no inbound-email-to-ticket parsing** anywhere in the codebase — I grepped every `worker/*.ts` and `lib/*.ts` file for writers of `TicketMessage` and `lib/actions-support.ts` is the only one. So today a customer cannot "reply to the email" and have it land in the ticket; they must go back to the portal. This matters for the Discord design: **Discord replying-back-to-customer will need the exact same "notify + link back to portal" shape**, not a new inbound-email channel, unless Nxeon wants to build that separately.

`createTicket` (line 53) and `setTicketStatus`/`setTicketPriority` (lines 165-191) are the other actions; all gate through `requireTicketActor()` (line 48), which resolves `canAccess(user.role, "support")` from `lib/rbac.ts`.

There is a **second, independent writer of `Ticket`**: the AI agent itself, via the `open_support_ticket` tool in `lib/kb-tools.ts:141-169`, executed by `openTicket()` — the bot can create tickets on a signed-in customer's behalf without going through `createTicket` in `actions-support.ts` at all. Any Discord relay of "new tickets" needs to catch both paths (or better, hook the relay at the DB-write layer / a single new helper both paths call, rather than duplicating relay logic in two callers).

### 1.2 Live chat — `lib/actions-chat.ts`, `lib/chat-bot-step.ts`, `lib/chat-attachment.ts`, `lib/chat-typing.ts`, `lib/support-promise.ts`

Schema: `ChatConversation` (`prisma/schema.prisma:2565-2586`) and `ChatMessage` (`:2588-2602`) — **not** "ChatSession", confirming the actual names to use in any new code. Key fields on `ChatConversation`: `visitorId` (anon cookie id), `userId` (nullable — set only if signed in), `status` ("OPEN"/"CLOSED", plain strings not an enum), `assignedToId` (staff user id), `unreadForAgent`/`unreadForUser`, and critically **`botEscalatedAt`** — a nullable timestamp with this exact comment in the schema (`:2577-2581`):

> "AI-assistant human-handoff window: set (atomically) when the bot escalates to a live agent and emails them. While set, the bot stays quiet waiting for a human; if the window elapses with no agent, the bot posts the 'no agents available' fallback."

`ChatAttachment` (`:2608-2616`) stores image bytes **in Postgres**, not on disk (comment explains the non-root web process can't write to disk) — relevant if Discord needs to relay images either direction; they'd need to be fetched from Postgres and re-uploaded to Discord, or Discord's CDN URLs downloaded and stored as new `ChatAttachment` rows.

`lib/actions-chat.ts` is the **entire admin-side chat interface**, and it is **100% polling, not websockets**: `listConversations()` (line 64) is explicitly commented "Polled by the client." `replyToConversation()` (line 136) does `chatMessage.create` + `chatConversation.update({ status: "OPEN", unreadForUser: true, assignedToId: staff.id })` in a transaction, then a best-effort `notification.create` if `convo.userId` is set. `replyWithAttachment` (line 190) is the same with an added `chatAttachment.create`, gated by `validateImageBytes` in `lib/chat-attachment.ts` (magic-number/allow-list/5MB cap, confirmed by reading the file's docstring at `lib/actions-chat.ts:184-189`). There's also `closeConversation`, `closeAllConversations`, `assignConversation`, and `signalAgentTyping` (writes to the in-memory `lib/chat-typing.ts` store, not the DB).

`lib/chat-bot-step.ts` is a **pure in-memory (not DB) "what is the bot doing right now" signal**, keyed by conversation id, TTL 9 seconds (`BOT_STEP_TTL_MS`), explicitly documented as acceptable only because "this app runs single-process" (line 9) — a real constraint if Nxeon ever horizontally scales, unrelated to Discord but worth knowing since a Discord bridge would add a second process (or at least a second write-path) touching the same conversations.

### 1.3 The AI agent — `lib/kb-llm.ts`, `lib/kb-run.ts`, `lib/kb-tools.ts`

This is the most important discovery for the "fully automated" question, and it directly contradicts assuming there's already a human interface beyond the admin panel — **there is exactly one human handoff mechanism today, and it's email.**

`lib/kb-run.ts` (`runAssistant`, lines 192-313) is the orchestrator both `/api/chat` and `/api/chat/upload` call. The policy, read directly from the code:
- The bot goes **silent forever** on a conversation the instant an agent message exists or `assignedToId` is set (line 217-218) — "Never talk over a human."
- **The bot never proactively offers a human.** Per the system prompt built in `lib/kb-llm.ts:149`: *"do your best to handle everything yourself... only when the visitor explicitly asks to talk to a person"* — confirmed again in `kb-run.ts:257-258`'s comment: "A live agent is ONLY brought in when the visitor explicitly asks for one (humanIntent → kind 'handoff'). The bot never offers or escalates on its own."
- When handoff triggers, `escalate()` (`kb-run.ts:105-142`) atomically claims `botEscalatedAt` via `updateMany({ where: { botEscalatedAt: null } })` (so concurrent triggers can't double-fire), posts a holding message ("Let me get a teammate for you... 👋"), and **emails one address** — `kb_bot_agent_email` setting, falling back to `support_email` — with a link to `/admin/chat`. That's it. No SMS, no Slack, no push notification, no Discord.
- `checkEscalationTimeout()` (line 150) — called on every message *and* every GET poll — checks if `kb_bot_window_sec` (admin setting, default **180 seconds**) has elapsed with no agent reply/assignment, and if so posts the "no agents available, we'll follow up within one business day" fallback (`NO_AGENT_MSG`, line 30) and clears the escalation flag.
- Guardrails: a per-conversation bot-reply cap (`kb_bot_max_replies`, default 16) that auto-escalates once hit, and a platform-wide daily paid-call cap (`kb_bot_daily_cap`) that degrades to a token-free retrieval answer once exceeded — both logged to `KbBotLog`.

`lib/support-promise.ts` is a small but telling file: it exists purely because a 2026-07-26 "journey rehearsal" found **four different, contradictory reply-time promises** across the site (24/7, "a few minutes," "a few hours," "one business day"), and the fix was to standardize on the *slowest, most honest* one — `SUPPORT_REPLY_WITHIN = "within one business day"` — with an explicit comment: *"nothing pages a human out of hours."* This is a direct, sourced admission in the codebase that **there is currently no out-of-hours paging of any kind** — the human-handoff email in `kb-run.ts` is best-effort and silent if nobody's watching their inbox. Any Discord integration pitched as improving responsiveness should be honest that it's competing with (and could genuinely fix) this exact gap, not with some already-robust escalation system.

`lib/kb-llm.ts:84-160` (`buildSystem`) is the full system prompt — confirms `accountAware` mode gives the bot read tools (`get_account_overview`, `list_services`, `get_service`, `list_invoices`, `get_billing_status`, `list_tickets`, `check_platform_status`, `get_plans`, `search_help`) plus exactly one write tool, `open_support_ticket` — "You can READ everything but you can only WRITE by opening a support ticket." This is the ceiling on what "AI does everything" can mean today without new tool grants: the bot cannot restart a server, issue a refund, or change settings from chat or (by extension) from Discord unless new tools are built.

`STEP_LABELS` (`kb-llm.ts:49-60`) map tool names to live-progress strings surfaced via `chat-bot-step.ts` — cosmetic, but shows the pattern for adding a Discord-specific step label later (e.g. "Posting to the team's Discord…").

### 1.4 Admin UI — `app/admin/chat/page.tsx`, `app/admin/support/`

`app/admin/chat/page.tsx` (75 lines) is a full server-rendered inbox: loads up to 200 conversations server-side, resolves `assignedToId` → staff name, computes `Open`/`Unread`/`Total` stat cards from real `count()` queries (not the capped 200-row list — explicit comment about this at line 17-19), and hands off to a client component `<ChatInbox initial={...}/>` (`components/admin/ChatInbox.tsx`, not read in full but referenced) which does the client-side polling and calls the `lib/actions-chat.ts` actions. `app/admin/support/page.tsx` and `app/admin/support/[id]/page.tsx` are the ticket-desk equivalent (111 + 138 lines).

**This means a Discord bridge is not filling an empty gap — a working, real-time-enough (polling) staff UI already exists for both surfaces.** Discord would be a second, parallel front-end onto the same rows, which is exactly the sync-consistency problem to design carefully (see §3.3): if a mod can reply from either Discord or `/admin/chat`/`/admin/support`, both paths must hit the same DB-write helper so state (status, `assignedToId`, unread flags, notifications, email) never diverges.

### 1.5 Existing webhook/integration precedent — Stripe/PayPal/Coinbase webhooks

No Slack/Discord/Zapier/generic-webhook integration exists anywhere in the codebase today (confirmed by an exhaustive grep — every Discord-related hit is either marketing copy for Nxeon's "Discord bot hosting" product page, `social_discord` (a plain URL string in `lib/settings.ts:50`, just a footer link, not an integration), or unrelated words like "slack"/"bot" in comments).

The real precedent for *inbound* signed webhooks is `app/api/stripe/webhook/route.ts:1-40`: reads the raw body as text, extracts a signature header (`stripe-signature`), verifies via `stripe().webhooks.constructEvent(raw, sig, secret)`, returns 400 on any failure, and — notably — **swallows internal processing errors deliberately** so Stripe's retry-on-non-2xx behavior doesn't cause duplicate side effects, relying on an idempotency key (`FulfilledSession` unique constraint) instead (see the comment block at lines 24-36). This is the pattern to imitate for `/api/webhooks/discord`: raw-body signature verification, fast/small response, DB-level idempotency rather than trusting "we returned 200 so it won't retry."

For secret storage, `lib/settings.ts` + `lib/actions-settings.ts` already have an admin-configurable **encrypted-secret settings** pattern used for `kb_bot_api_key` (`actions-settings.ts:314`, `type: "secret"`, encrypted via `encryptSecret()` from `lib/crypto-box.ts` before being stored, decrypted via `decryptSecret()` in `kb-llm.ts:69`). `crypto-box.ts:1-40` is AES-256-GCM keyed off `scryptSync(AUTH_SECRET, "nxeon-byok", 32)`. **This is the natural home for a Discord bot token / public key / webhook URL** — an admin settings field, not a hardcoded env var, so it can be rotated without a redeploy (though a fallback `process.env.DISCORD_BOT_TOKEN` mirroring `resolveBotKey()`'s pattern in `kb-llm.ts:67-73` is reasonable too).

### 1.6 Architecture constraint that matters most: no persistent process for a Gateway connection, but a real background worker exists

`app/api/chat/route.ts:1-60` confirms the customer-facing chat endpoint is plain Next.js `runtime = "nodejs"` request/response — POST to send, GET to poll (`app/api/chat/route.ts` docstring, lines 12-16). There is **no websocket server** for chat (the `ws` package in `package.json` is present but not used for this feature — not verified further, out of scope here). This means Nxeon's whole live surface (customer widget *and* admin inbox) is built on short-lived HTTP requests, never a long-lived connection.

Separately, `worker/index.ts` (imports on lines 1-51) is a genuine **long-running Node process** — `npm run worker` → `tsx worker/index.ts`, a job-queue loop polling every `POLL_MS = 3000` (line 56) plus dozens of periodic "sweep" functions (`billingSweep`, `monitorSweep`, `sslSweep`, etc.) imported and presumably invoked in a loop later in the file. **This is the one place in the codebase that already behaves like a daemon**, and is the natural home for either (a) a Discord Gateway client (if chosen) or (b) a new `discordRelaySweep()` polling function that fits the exact same idiom as everything else in that file. This detail should directly drive the Part 3 recommendation below.

---

## Part 2 — External research (Discord platform + comparable products), sourced

### 2.1 Discord platform capabilities, verified against current docs

**Forum channels cannot have private threads — this is confirmed, current, and changes the design.** Per `docs.discord.com/developers/topics/threads` (fetched directly): "Forum channels only support public threads... private threads are exclusively created in `GUILD_TEXT` channels." This kills the naive "one ticket = one private forum thread" idea. The two real options are:
1. A **forum channel restricted at the guild-role level** (only a "Support Staff" Discord role can even view the channel) with one **public-within-that-channel** post per ticket — fine, because no customer is ever a member of that channel in the staff-side-only design (§Design A below). Forum posts support `available_tags` (status labels like Open/Waiting/Closed) and a `REQUIRE_TAG` flag, and auto-archive on inactivity unless pinned (source: `docs.discord.com/developers/topics/threads`).
2. **Private text-channel-per-ticket with permission overwrites** (owner + staff role only) — the pattern every mainstream OSS Discord ticket bot actually uses (see §2.3). This is required only if real Discord users (customers) need to be scoped out of each other's tickets, i.e. only matters for Design B.

**Webhooks vs. bot messages.** Incoming webhooks are channel-scoped HTTP POST endpoints requiring no persistent connection and no bot user at all — good for one-way notifications (source: Hookdeck's Discord webhook guide, cross-checked against Discord's own webhook docs page). They render as messages "from" the webhook's configured name/avatar, not as a real bot user, and **cannot read anything back** — "bots can read and write, webhooks can only write" (same source). Critically, Discord's `Execute Webhook` endpoint *does* support posting into a forum channel and creating a new thread there via a `thread_name` parameter — meaning the "post the customer's opening message as a new ticket" step could, in principle, be done via a webhook without needing full bot REST calls, though a bot token is still needed for anything that reads messages back or manages channel permissions.

**Discord Components v2 / interactions.** Confirmed current (docs updated through April 2026, per `docs.discord.com/developers/components/reference` via DeepWiki cross-reference): buttons, select menus, and modals (`Text Input` components, modal-only) remain the interaction primitives. Components v2 adds `Text Display`, `Container`, `Media Gallery`, `Thumbnail`, gated behind an `IS_COMPONENTS_V2` message flag that, once set on a message, is permanent for that message and disables the old `content`/`embeds` fields in favor of the new component types. A "Reply" button under a mirrored customer message → opens a modal → mod types text → submits — is a fully supported, current interaction pattern.

**Interactions are signed with Ed25519, and this is mandatory, not optional.** Confirmed via `discord.com/developers/docs/interactions/overview` (redirects to `docs.discord.com`) and the `discord-interactions-js` reference: every interaction POST carries `X-Signature-Ed25519` and `X-Signature-Timestamp` headers; the receiving endpoint must verify by concatenating timestamp + raw body and checking against the app's public key, returning **401** on failure. Discord will refuse to save an Interactions Endpoint URL in the Developer Portal if it doesn't pass a live verification check, and it periodically re-tests the endpoint with deliberately invalid signatures. This is directly analogous to (and should mirror) the Stripe webhook pattern in `app/api/stripe/webhook/route.ts` — raw body, header-based signature, 400/401 on failure.

**HTTP-only bots are a real, supported deployment mode.** A bot can operate entirely via (a) an Interactions Endpoint URL for slash commands/buttons/modals and (b) plain REST calls (create channel, post message) triggered from Nxeon's own server actions — **with no persistent Gateway/WebSocket connection at all** — as long as it never needs to react to a plain, non-interaction message a human just types into a channel. This is the single most important design lever: if mods are asked to reply via a button→modal flow (not by just typing in the channel), Nxeon never needs to run a discord.js Gateway client or any new always-on process; the entire bridge can live as ordinary Next.js API routes plus REST calls, matching the existing architecture. If instead the goal is "a mod can just type normally in the ticket channel," Nxeon needs either (i) a persistent Gateway connection (a real new long-running process — natural home is `worker/index.ts`, since that's already the one daemon in this codebase) or (ii) a periodic **REST poll** of each active ticket's channel (`GET /channels/{id}/messages?after=<last_id>`) from the existing `worker/index.ts` sweep loop — no Gateway needed, just another sweep function using the exact `POLL_MS`-style idiom already used everywhere else in that file. Given this codebase's dominant idiom is polling (chat widget polls, admin inbox polls, worker sweeps poll), **the REST-poll-from-worker approach is the most architecturally consistent, not the Gateway approach** — this is a genuine, non-generic recommendation grounded in what's actually in `worker/index.ts` today, not a default "just use discord.js" answer.

**Rate limits.** Confirmed via `docs.discord.com/developers/topics/rate-limits`: a global rate limit of 50 requests/second per bot/app, plus separate per-route limits (bucketed, surfaced via `X-RateLimit-Bucket`/`X-RateLimit-Remaining` response headers). At any realistic Nxeon support volume (dozens to low hundreds of concurrent tickets, not thousands of messages/second), this is not a practical constraint — worth stating plainly rather than treating as a risk.

**Verification / privileged intents — genuinely good news for this specific use case.** Two separate thresholds, confirmed via `support-dev.discord.com` articles (cross-referenced, dated June 10, 2026 policy change):
- **Bot (app) verification** is required once a bot is in **100+ servers**. Nxeon's support bot lives in exactly **one** private guild (its own support server) — this threshold will never be hit for Design A, and only matters if Nxeon later runs the *same* bot inside a separate large public community server (Part 4).
- **Privileged Gateway Intents** (`GUILD_PRESENCES`, `MESSAGE_CONTENT`, `GUILD_MEMBERS`) previously required Discord approval once a bot was in 100+ servers; as of the June 2026 change, the threshold is now **10,000 unique users who can see the app across all its servers** — a private staff-only support guild with a handful to a few dozen staff members will never approach this. **Conclusion: Nxeon's Discord support bridge, scoped to a single private server, needs no Discord bot verification and no privileged-intent review at all** — this removes what is often the single biggest lead-time risk (Discord's app review queue) for this specific design. This flips only if Nxeon also builds the public community server from Part 4 and that server grows past ~10k members with the same bot installed and `MESSAGE_CONTENT` enabled.

**ToS/Developer Policy — real, sourced, and mostly favorable, with two clauses worth flagging.** From Discord's Developer Policy (cross-referenced via `support-dev.discord.com/hc/.../8563934450327-Discord-Developer-Policy` and the mirrored `discord-api-docs` GitHub source):
- *"You may not use message content obtained through the APIs to train machine learning or AI models (including large language models) unless express permission is granted by Discord."* — This matters only if Nxeon later wants to fine-tune or otherwise train the support AI on historical Discord message content harvested via the bot. **Using message content to relay it live (forward to the DB, forward to the customer) is ordinary bot functionality and is not "training a model" — that's fine.** Flag this explicitly if anyone proposes training the KB/AI agent on a corpus of past Discord support threads.
- *"You may not contact users outside of Discord without their explicit consent by using any API Data."* — In Design A (customer never touches Discord; their email/identity come from Nxeon's own `User` table, not from Discord's API), this clause simply doesn't apply — no Discord API data about the customer exists. It becomes directly relevant only if Nxeon later adds Discord-OAuth account linking (Part 4) and then wants to, say, email or DM a customer using data obtained via their linked Discord identity — that would need the OAuth consent screen to clearly disclose it, which is standard practice and low-risk if done properly, but should not be skipped.
- I found **no clause anywhere in the current policy or ToS specifically prohibiting "using a private Discord server as an internal support-ops tool for a separate paying product"** — this is an extremely common, long-standing pattern (every OSS ticket bot below exists for exactly this) and is not something Discord's policy singles out. I'm flagging this as verified-against-current-policy-text rather than assumed, per the task's sourcing requirement, but note I could not access Discord's Developer ToS page directly (it 403'd for automated fetch) and instead cross-verified policy language through Discord's own GitHub-mirrored policy doc and secondary summaries — **treat the "no prohibition found" conclusion as reasonably but not 100% independently confirmed; worth a final human read of `support-dev.discord.com/hc/en-us/articles/8562894815383` before committing engineering time**, exactly per the instruction to flag anything not fully verifiable.

### 2.2 How comparable companies actually bridge Discord and a "real" helpdesk

- **Chatwoot** (open-source, self-hosted helpdesk, a fair architectural peer to Nxeon's own custom system) has **no first-party bidirectional Discord channel** — it's a community-maintained bolt-on, `discord-tickets/chatwoot-modmail` on GitHub (public, GPL-3.0, low-activity — 1 commit, 5 stars at the time of checking, so treat it as a reference architecture, not a production-hardened dependency to adopt wholesale). Chatwoot's own GitHub issue tracker (`chatwoot/chatwoot#1941`, tagged CW-2873) shows Discord integration as a **long-standing open feature request**, not a shipped core capability. This is a meaningful data point: even a company whose entire product *is* a helpdesk has not built genuine two-way Discord sync as a first-party feature — it's routinely left to bolt-ons or Zapier/Pabbly-style one-directional automation ("new Chatwoot conversation → post to Discord channel," not a real round trip).
- **Zendesk/Intercom/Freshdesk/Help Scout**: no evidence found of a genuine bidirectional Discord bridge as a native feature in any of them either — what exists is one-directional notification integration (post ticket events into a Discord channel) via generic webhook/Zapier connectors, the same shallow pattern. **Nobody in the mainstream helpdesk-SaaS space has actually solved this as a polished first-party product feature** — which means Nxeon building this is a genuine differentiator for a hosting company whose audience is Discord-native, not "catching up" to an existing standard.
- **The real prior art is the OSS Discord ticket-bot ecosystem**, purpose-built for exactly this shape of problem: `Ticket Tool` (claims 1.8M+ active servers, 500M+ users, 180M+ tickets — a Discord App Directory listing, so treat the usage numbers as marketing but the product category as real and mature), `Tickets` (`tickets.bot`), `Discord Tickets` (`discordtickets.app`, "free alternative to premium... plans of Ticket Tool, TicketsBot, Tickety, Helper.gg"), and `Open Ticket` (`open-discord-bots/open-ticket` on GitHub, explicitly built to also integrate with Pterodactyl — the exact game-server-panel software Nxeon's own audience is adjacent to). Their shared, converged architecture (confirmed across multiple of these sources): **a private text channel per ticket** (not a forum thread) under a "Tickets" category, named e.g. `support-<username>`, with permission overwrites granting access only to the ticket's opener + a staff role; a "claim" button a mod clicks to self-assign; a "close" button that generates an **HTML transcript** and archives/deletes the channel. This is structurally the closest existing analog to "customer messages support → Discord thread → mod replies → customer gets it back" described in the prompt, and it's worth explicitly building Nxeon's Design B (if pursued) as a thin variant of this exact, already-proven pattern rather than inventing a new one.
- Notably, **`Ticket Tool` now advertises "AI assistance"** in its own marketing copy (`ticket-tool.app`) — independent confirmation that "AI inside a Discord ticket bot" is now a normal, expected feature in this exact product category by 2026, not a novel idea Nxeon would be first to try.
- On the "hosting/game-server companies actually run big public Discord servers with visible ticket systems" point: this is genuinely, visibly true for essentially every mid-size Minecraft/game-server host (BisectHosting, Shockbyte, Apex Hosting, and dozens of smaller ones all run large public Discord communities with ticket-bot-style support channels alongside a separate web dashboard for billing) — but I could not find a citable, verified *written source* describing any specific one's internal architecture beyond what's directly observable by joining their server, so I'm stating this as well-known industry practice rather than a sourced technical claim, and recommend not citing specific competitors' internals as fact in any customer-facing copy without firsthand verification.

### 2.3 Is "fully automated" realistic, and what does AI-in-Discord actually look like

The current industry-standard pattern, confirmed via Zendesk and Intercom's own current pricing/product pages (2026): **"AI copilot drafts, human approves"** is a distinct, actively-sold tier from "AI agent resolves autonomously." Concretely: Intercom's Fin **Copilot** ($35/user/month) "drafts replies, summarizes threads, retrieves internal content for human teammates" while its separate Fin **AI Agent** is billed per resolved outcome ($0.99/outcome) for fully autonomous handling. Zendesk's equivalent **Copilot** ($50/agent/month add-on) explicitly "helps agents draft the perfect reply... suggest next steps, draft responses, and execute approved actions," again as a human-in-the-loop layer distinct from Zendesk's separate autonomous AI Agents. This validates the phased design in Part 3: full autonomy and copilot-style drafting are treated industry-wide as **separate product tiers with separate risk profiles**, not a single on/off switch — Nxeon should build the same distinction rather than jumping straight to "AI replies to Discord customers with no human in the loop."

Given Nxeon's own `kb-llm.ts`/`kb-run.ts` architecture (documented in §1.3): the AI agent today can already read a customer's full account state and open a ticket, but its only write action is ticket-creation, and it is explicitly forbidden from restarting servers, issuing refunds, or changing settings. **"Fully automated" cannot mean "the AI closes the loop end-to-end from Discord" without first deciding whether to grant it new write tools** (restart-service, apply-refund, etc.) — a much bigger, separate decision from "let Discord see it." Realistically, "fully automated" for the *Discord bridge specifically* should mean: the human-handoff email (`kb-run.ts:117-137`) is replaced/supplemented by a Discord post, and/or the AI drafts a suggested reply as a Discord message a mod can click to send verbatim or edit — not that Discord independently makes decisions AI doesn't already make elsewhere in the product today.

## Part 3 — Concrete architecture proposal

### 3.1 Two designs — pick Design A first

**Design A — Staff-only relay/bridge (recommended starting point).** Customers never see or touch Discord. Every `Ticket`/`ChatConversation` gets mirrored, on creation, into a single private Discord guild that only Nxeon staff belong to. A mod's reply in Discord round-trips into the real DB and out to the customer exactly the way a reply typed into `/admin/chat` or `/admin/support` does today — same DB writes, same email, same notification. Discord becomes a third front-end onto the existing data, alongside the two that already exist.

**Design B — Discord as an additional customer entry point (optional, later phase).** A public/semi-public Discord server where a customer can open a ticket via a button (creating a private text channel, per the OSS pattern in §2.2) or DM a bot for modmail-style support, in addition to the website widget. This requires solving Discord-identity ↔ Nxeon-account linking (OAuth) if any account-specific action is needed, and needs the private-channel-per-ticket pattern rather than the shared-forum-channel pattern used in Design A, since real, distinct Discord users (customers) now need to be isolated from each other.

Recommendation: **build Design A completely (through Phase 3 below) before touching Design B.** Design A alone answers the owner's actual ask ("relays the info... sends replies back through the Nxeon system"); Design B is a genuinely separate product decision (does Nxeon want customers *inside* its Discord at all, moderation overhead, spam/abuse surface) that shouldn't be pre-committed to just because the bridge exists.

### 3.2 Data flow (Design A), in words

**Customer → Discord:**
1. Customer submits a ticket (`createTicket` in `lib/actions-support.ts:53`, or the AI's `openTicket` tool in `lib/kb-tools.ts`) or sends a live-chat message (`/api/chat` → `runAssistant` in `lib/kb-run.ts`).
2. A new, single relay helper (not duplicated across both callers — see §3.3) checks a `discordChannelId`/`discordThreadId` field on the row (new schema field, see §3.3). If null, it calls Discord's REST API to `POST` a new forum thread (or channel) into the staff-only Discord support guild, titled with the ticket subject / conversation visitor name, and stores the returned thread id back onto the `Ticket`/`ChatConversation` row.
3. The message body (plus any attachment, downloaded from Postgres via `ChatAttachment`/none-yet-for-tickets and re-uploaded to Discord) is posted into that thread as the first message, formatted with the customer's name/email/plan context pulled from the same DB the AI agent already has read-tools for (`get_account_overview` etc. in `lib/kb-tools.ts`) — this is a good reuse point rather than writing new lookup logic.
4. Subsequent customer messages on the same ticket/conversation post as additional messages in the same Discord thread.

**Mod replies in Discord → customer:**
5. A mod, in the Discord thread, clicks a "Reply" button attached to the bot's message (Components v2 button + modal, per §2.1) and types their reply, **or** (if Nxeon accepts the extra engineering cost of a worker-based poller or Gateway connection) just types a normal message in the thread.
6. That reply is delivered to Nxeon either as a signed HTTP interaction (`MODAL_SUBMIT`, verified via Ed25519 at a new `app/api/webhooks/discord` route, mirroring the Stripe webhook's raw-body-plus-signature pattern) or picked up by a new `worker/index.ts` sweep function polling `GET /channels/{id}/messages` for each active thread.
7. Nxeon calls the **same underlying write path** `replyTicket`/`replyToConversation` already use — i.e., refactor a shared internal function (e.g. `applyTicketReply(ticketId, body, { asStaffId })`) that both the existing server actions and the new Discord path call, so status transitions, `db.notification.create`, and `sendMail(emails.ticketReply(...))` all fire exactly once regardless of which surface the reply came from. This is the single most important implementation discipline: **do not write a second, parallel "Discord version" of the reply logic** — that's how the two front-ends drift out of sync.
8. The customer sees the reply the same way they always have: an in-app notification bell, an email with a link back to `/dashboard/support/[id]` or the chat widget, and the row itself updated (`status: ANSWERED` / `unreadForUser: true`).
9. The bot posts a small confirmation back into the Discord thread ("✅ sent to the customer") so the mod knows the round trip completed — this is a UX nicety, not a data-flow requirement.

### 3.3 What needs to be built

- **New Discord application** in the Developer Portal: bot token + public key (for Ed25519 verification) + (optionally) an OAuth2 client if Design B account-linking is ever pursued. Stored via the existing encrypted-settings pattern (`lib/settings.ts` + `lib/actions-settings.ts`, `type: "secret"`, `encryptSecret`/`decryptSecret` from `lib/crypto-box.ts` — same pattern as `kb_bot_api_key`), not a bare env var, so it's admin-rotatable.
- **New webhook/interactions receiver**: `app/api/webhooks/discord/route.ts`. Must (a) read the raw body as text before any JSON parsing (Ed25519 verification needs the exact raw bytes, same lesson as Stripe's `req.text()` in `app/api/stripe/webhook/route.ts:13`), (b) verify `X-Signature-Ed25519`/`X-Signature-Timestamp` against the bot's public key, returning 401 on failure, (c) handle Discord's `PING` interaction type (required for Discord to accept the endpoint URL at all), (d) route `MODAL_SUBMIT`/`MESSAGE_COMPONENT` interactions to the shared reply-write helper described above.
- **Schema change** (new Prisma fields, additive/nullable so no backfill is required): `Ticket.discordThreadId String?` and `ChatConversation.discordThreadId String?` (plus maybe `discordChannelId` if using channel-per-ticket instead of forum-thread-per-ticket). This is the "join-table/field" the prompt asked about — a field is simpler and sufficient here since it's a strict 1:1 relationship; a join table would only be needed if a single ticket could map to multiple Discord threads, which there's no reason to support.
- **A relay/mirror function**, called from both `createTicket` (`lib/actions-support.ts:53`) and `openTicket` (`lib/kb-tools.ts`'s tool executor) for tickets, and from the point where a new `ChatConversation` first gets a message (likely inside `runAssistant`/the `/api/chat` POST handler) for chat — this is genuinely two integration points to update per surface (ticket has two writers, chat effectively has one visitor-facing entry), not one.
- **The reply round-trip**, per §3.2 step 7 — requires refactoring `replyTicket` (`lib/actions-support.ts:87-149`) and `replyToConversation` (`lib/actions-chat.ts:136-181`) to expose an internal, non-"use server" function the Discord webhook handler can also call directly (a "use server" file can only export async functions callable from client components; a Discord webhook route calling into the same logic needs a plain importable function, so this is a real, non-trivial refactor of two existing, currently-working, well-tested files — not just "add a new file").
- **Either a `worker/index.ts` polling sweep** (if replies should support plain typed messages, not just button/modal) **or accept button+modal-only replies** (if the HTTP-only, no-new-process design is preferred). Given the codebase's existing idiom (§1.6, §2.1), the button+modal approach that needs zero new long-running processes is the lower-risk, lower-effort starting point; a polling sweep or Gateway client can be added later if mods find modals too clunky for fast back-and-forth.
- **Where the AI plugs in**: two independent options, not mutually exclusive — (i) the existing `runAssistant`/`escalate()` flow in `lib/kb-run.ts:105-142` gets a second notification channel: instead of (or in addition to) emailing `kb_bot_agent_email`, it posts into the Discord thread ("🔔 wants a human") — this is a **small, additive change to an already-existing, already-tested function**, genuinely low-effort; (ii) an AI-drafted-reply feature where, when a mod opens a ticket's thread, the bot posts a suggested reply (reusing `llmAnswer`/`askClaudeWithTools` from `lib/kb-llm.ts`) with a "Send as-is" / "Edit then send" button pair — this is new logic, not just wiring, and belongs in Phase 3 below.

### 3.4 Security/privacy considerations specific to Nxeon

- **Scope the entire support relay into one guild, one role.** Every ticket/chat thread lives in a channel/category visible only to a Discord role like `@Support Staff` — never `@everyone`. This is a Discord server-configuration step, not code, but must be documented as a hard operational requirement, and revisited any time a new Discord member is added to the guild for any reason (community management, marketing, etc.) — the guild used for support should ideally be a **separate guild** from any future public community server (Part 4), specifically so "who's in our public Discord" and "who can see customer PII" are never the same access-control question.
- **Redact or omit sensitive fields by default.** The relay message posted per-ticket should show name/email/plan/service-id (already what the AI agent surfaces to itself via `get_account_overview` etc.) but should **never** include anything payment-adjacent — Nxeon's Stripe/PayPal/Coinbase integrations (`app/api/*/webhook/route.ts`) never expose raw card data to the app layer at all (standard for those providers), so there's nothing to leak there by default, but a deliberate rule ("never paste a customer's raw address, phone, or full payment-method fingerprint into Discord even if a tool can see it") should be enforced in whatever template builds the relay message.
- **Audit log.** Every reply sent via Discord should be attributed to the real Nxeon staff user who authorized it, not "the bot" or a raw Discord username — this requires **Discord-account ↔ Nxeon-staff-account linking** for every mod (a small one-time OAuth linking step per staff member, using Nxeon's existing `User`/`Role` model, `SUPPORT`/`ADMIN` roles per `prisma/schema.prisma:10-15` and `lib/rbac.ts:26-29`), so `TicketMessage.authorId`/whatever chat-message author field is used records the real Nxeon user, not a synthetic "discord-bot" account. This also directly enables the existing `requireTicketActor()`/`requireArea("support")` guards to keep working unchanged for Discord-originated replies.
- **Revoking access.** When a support staff member leaves, removing them from the Discord guild (or the `@Support Staff` role) should be a required step in the same offboarding checklist as revoking their Nxeon admin-panel role — this bridge doubles the places PII access needs to be revoked, and should be called out explicitly in whatever offboarding doc/process exists (not found in this audit; worth confirming one exists at all, independent of Discord).
- **Rate-limit and validate the webhook route** exactly like every other public-facing Nxeon webhook (`checkRateLimit`, used elsewhere e.g. `lib/actions-chat.ts:196`) — Discord's signature verification stops forged requests, but a compromised or buggy Discord-side automation could still hammer the endpoint.

### 3.5 Phased rollout, with an honest effort assessment

**Phase 1 — Read-only mirror (quick build, low risk).** New tickets/conversations post into Discord automatically; no reply path yet. This is genuinely the "quick" phase: it touches `createTicket`, `openTicket`, and the chat entry point to add a relay call, needs the schema field, needs Discord REST calls for thread creation, and needs no signature verification or webhook receiver at all (pure outbound). **Effort: small — a few days of focused work**, most of it in getting the Discord REST plumbing (bot token, thread creation, message formatting) right and testing against real rate limits/edge cases (thread creation failures, Discord API downtime — must be best-effort/non-blocking exactly like the existing `sendMail` calls in `actions-support.ts:116-135` and `kb-run.ts`'s escalation email, which are all wrapped in try/catch specifically so a third-party failure never breaks the primary flow).

**Phase 2 — Reply round-trip (the real engineering effort).** Mod replies in Discord (button+modal) land back in the DB and reach the customer. This is where the actual complexity is concentrated: (a) the Ed25519-verified webhook receiver is new infrastructure with a real security requirement to get right; (b) `replyTicket`/`replyToConversation` need refactoring into a shared, callable-from-anywhere core so both front-ends stay in sync — this touches two files that are currently working, tested, RBAC-audited code (note `actions-support.ts`'s own docstring at lines 11-33 describing a *previous* RBAC bug in this exact file — this file has already had one subtle authorization bug; refactor it carefully and re-run whatever test covers `test/auth-lockouts.test.ts`, referenced at `actions-support.ts:37`); (c) Discord-account-to-Nxeon-staff-account linking needs building (a small OAuth flow, but a genuinely new auth surface); (d) idempotency/race handling for "mod replies from Discord at the same moment another mod replies from `/admin/support`" needs explicit handling (last-write-wins on `status` is probably fine, given the existing code already tolerates similar races via `updateMany`-based claiming elsewhere, e.g. `kb-run.ts:106-110`, `:173-176`). **Effort: substantial — this is the core of the project**, likely the majority of total engineering time, and the piece most likely to reveal edge cases in testing (attachments round-tripping, thread-vs-ticket state drift, Discord API outages mid-reply).

**Phase 3 — AI-drafted replies with mod approval.** Reuses `lib/kb-llm.ts`'s existing `llmAnswer`/`askClaudeWithTools` machinery (already grounded, already tool-using, already has an account-aware mode) to post a suggested reply into the thread with Send/Edit buttons. **Effort: moderate** — the LLM plumbing already exists and is proven in production for the chat widget; the new work is entirely UI/interaction-flow (rendering the suggestion, wiring the buttons to the same reply-write path from Phase 2) plus a new system-prompt variant tuned for "draft an internal-facing reply for a human to check" rather than "reply directly to the customer."

**Phase 4 — Deeper automation / optional Design B.** Expanding the AI's write-tool set (restart-service, apply-credit, etc.) so it can act with less human involvement, and/or opening a customer-facing Design B entry point in a separate community guild. **Effort: large and genuinely open-ended** — this is a product-strategy decision (how much autonomous action is the business comfortable granting an LLM) more than a pure engineering task, and should not be scoped or estimated until Phases 1-3 are live and the team has real data on how often AI-drafted replies get sent unedited.

**Honest risk concentration**: the risk is almost entirely in Phase 2 (the refactor of two live, RBAC-sensitive files, plus new signed-webhook infrastructure, plus a new cross-system identity-linking flow), not in the Discord API integration itself, which — per the sourced research in Part 2 — is well-documented, unlikely to need special Discord approval given the single-private-guild scope, and has generous rate limits for support-scale volume.

## Part 4 — Other features worth adding (prioritized, grounded in real Nxeon infrastructure)

1. **Automated incident alerts to Discord (quick win, high value).** Nxeon already has a real `StatusIncident` model (`prisma/schema.prisma:3015-3028`) with an `auto: Boolean` field distinguishing automatically-opened incidents from operator-opened ones, and a public `/app/status/page.tsx`. Wiring `StatusIncident` create/resolve events to post into a `#status-alerts` Discord channel via a simple **incoming webhook** (no bot, no signature verification needed on Nxeon's side since it's purely outbound) is genuinely one of the lowest-effort, most clearly-valuable additions on this whole list — it reuses data that already exists and needs no new bot infrastructure at all. Recommend building this *before* the support bridge itself, as a low-risk way to stand up "Nxeon posting into Discord" plumbing that Phase 1 of the bridge can then reuse.
2. **A public Discord community server, kept structurally separate from the private support-bridge guild.** Justified by real, verifiable audience fit: Nxeon's own marketing pages already sell "Discord bot hosting" as a product (`app/(marketing)/discord-bot-hosting/page.tsx`) and reference Discord repeatedly across game-hosting content (`prisma/seed-gamemods.ts`'s DiscordSRV/Discord-Chat mod listings, `prisma/seed-blog-gaming.ts`), confirming the target customer is already Discord-native. A community server (general chat, showcase channels, a role for paying customers) is a marketing/retention play, not a support mechanism, and should not share infrastructure or a guild with the private support bridge (§3.4).
3. **Self-service Discord slash commands for account status (e.g. `/server-status`, `/my-services`) — but gated behind real OAuth account linking, not raw Discord-identity trust.** The moment a Discord command can reveal or act on account data, Discord identity must be cryptographically linked to a Nxeon `User.id` via OAuth (Discord's standard OAuth2 flow, `identify` scope at minimum) with an explicit consent step — never inferred from a Discord username/nickname, which is trivially spoofable. Given Nxeon's AI agent already has exactly this read-tool surface (`get_account_overview`, `list_services`, `get_service`, `list_invoices`, `get_billing_status` in `lib/kb-tools.ts`), a linked Discord command could call the *same* tool-execution functions rather than duplicating account-lookup logic — genuinely low incremental effort once linking exists, but the linking flow itself is a real new auth surface (comparable in scope to Phase 2's staff-linking work) and should reuse it rather than building two separate Discord-OAuth flows.
4. **Referral/affiliate integration.** Nxeon already has a full affiliate system (`lib/affiliate.ts`, `lib/actions-affiliate.ts`, `app/dashboard/affiliate/`, `app/admin/affiliate/`) and a separate partner-commission system (`lib/partner-commission.ts`, `lib/partner.ts`). A Discord angle here (e.g., a `/referral-link` command, or auto-posting new-signup/commission milestones to a private affiliate-team channel) is a real, low-effort extension of existing infrastructure, but is a marketing/growth feature, not a support feature — sequence it independently of the support bridge.
5. **Public roadmap/changelog bot.** Lower priority: no existing Nxeon data model for a public roadmap/changelog was found in this audit (only `ROADMAP.md` exists, per the `ls` at the repo root — a static internal file, not a customer-facing feature), so this would be new product surface, not a bridge onto something that already exists. Worth doing eventually for a Discord-native audience, but it's a net-new feature to design from scratch, not a "wire up existing data" quick win like items 1 and 4.

**Explicitly not recommended, or recommended only with heavy caveats:** letting Discord slash commands perform *destructive* account actions (restart/reinstall/delete a server) directly — even with OAuth linking, the blast radius of a compromised Discord account or a social-engineered mod click is worse than the current dashboard-only flow, and the AI agent itself is deliberately scoped away from these actions today (`kb-llm.ts:92`, "you cannot yourself restart a server, issue a refund, cancel, or change settings"). Any future expansion of AI or Discord write-capability into destructive actions should be a separate, carefully-scoped decision — not bundled into the support-bridge project.
